column11: Rosh Hashanah 10b: ‘Rather, what opinion does it follow? column11: Shabbat 53b: ‘Rav Yosef said: Have you removed the tanna’im from the world? Rabbi Yosei Rabbi Yosei prohibits the animals from going out with all of these items, as he considers them burdens, except for the ewes that are kevunot. Rabbi Yehuda says: Goats may go out on Shabbat with their udders bound to dry their milk supply and discontinue their lactation in order to facilitate conception, as in that case, they are tied with a tight, permanent knot. However, they may not go out with their udders bound to conserve the milk, as in that case they are bound loosely. Apparently, there are tanna’im who rule leniently with regard to attaching pouches to the udders of goats and permit the practice, and others prohibit doing so.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 53b) to illuminate his exposition here (“Rather: "The Holy One does not perform a miracle for falsehood" (Shabbat 53b), all being executed in justice; and when salvation occurs outside strict desert, this is termed a pele [wonder]:...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And in Shabbat [53b]: "How deficient is this man that the orders of Creation were altered for him," showing on the contrary that for a deficient person against whom there were many accusers on high, preventing help through natural means to grant relief, there was a need to perform a great miracle that transcends the natural order entrusted to nature's intermediaries, where the power of the accusers cannot reach], and in Shabbat [32a]: "One should not descend into a place of danger expecting a miracle to be performed for him," which refers specifically to definite danger, for why should one rely on a miracle when there is merely a remote apprehension of danger?
column15: Therefore Rabbi Yitzchak challenged: The Torah should not have begun except from “This month shall be unto you”—what is the reason? Because it is the renewal of the moon; meaning that there begins the measure of holiness which the Blessed Name grants to Israel, to each according to his personal spiritual level, for there the matter is bound to the Holy One, blessed be He.

column15: And as it is written (Genesis 2:6): “And a mist went up from the earth”—referring to the yearning cry rising from the shattered worlds, as taught in Tikkunei HaZohar (Tikkun 52, 87a): “Ed” represents the letters Aleph-Dalet of the Name Adonai; come and see: an arousal from below to above is required first, and only afterward “and watered the whole face of the ground.”

column11: Deuteronomy 1:1: ‘These are the words that Moses addressed to all Israel on the other side of the Jordan.—Through the wilderness, in the Arabah near Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Di-zahab,’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 1:1) to illuminate his exposition here (“meriting to proclaim "These are the words" (Devarim 1:1) once he attained the words of Torah, as taught in Devarim Rabbah (1:1); and as is known from the Zohar (II, 25b) that in Egypt speech was...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: “Tophel, and Laban, and Di-zahav” Deuteronomy 1:1: Moses did not explicitly name the historical places of sin, because in those very locations Israel also performed good deeds: the Golden Calf occurred at Mount Sinai where they accepted the Torah; and in the place where they spoke against the manna—subsequently during the plague of fiery serpents they subjected their hearts to the Omnipresent Rosh Hashanah 29a.
column15: Prior to creation existence was like a wilderness, where divine providence was not overtly discerned, for before creation Hashem was termed “He” (Hu). And likewise in the Wilderness Generation, who clarified through faith that even in the barren desert Hashem sustains life, and through this acquired the Land of Israel, concerning which it is written (Deuteronomy 11:12): “A land which the Lord your God cares for continually”—where it is visibly manifest that Hashem sustains, and He is addressed directly as “You” (Attah).

column11: Devarim Rabbah 1:1: ‘“These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan; in the wilderness, in the Arava, opposite the Red Sea, between Paran and Tofel, and Laban, and Hatzerot, and Di Zahav” (Deuteronomy 1:1). “These are the words” – halakha: Is it permissible for a person of Israel to write a Torah scroll in any language? This is what the sages taught: The difference between Torah scrolls and phylacteries and mezuzot is only that Torah scrolls may be written in any language. Rabban Gamliel says: Even Torah scrolls, the Sages permitted to be written only in Greek.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Devarim Rabbah 1:1) to illuminate his exposition here (“meriting to proclaim "These are the words" (Devarim 1:1) once he attained the words of Torah, as taught in Devarim Rabbah (1:1); and as is known from the Zohar (II, 25b) that in Egypt speech was...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column15: “And the whole earth was of one language and of one speech.” In Midrash Rabbah (38:4) and Tanchuma here: This is what Solomon said (Proverbs 27:22): “Though you bray a fool in a mortar among crushed grain with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.”

column11: Zohar, Vaera 6:65-7:71: ‘When Moses came, the Voice appeared, but it was “a voice without speech”. This lasted until Israel approached Mount Sinai to receive the Torah. Then the Voice was united with the Utterance, and the word was spoken, as it says, “and the Lord spake all these words” (Ex. xx, I). column13: That is, every detail of their labor reflected the authentic will of the Blessed Name, and the labor with mortar was itself the hermeneutic measure of kal va-chomer, only that then it was cloaked in exile and degradation; yet they recognized this, and "sighed... and cried" that it be openly revealed that I, Hashem, dwell within the children of Israel.
column15: And the Gemara distinguishes (48a): where words were accompanied by money, the curse of “He who took retribution” applies; where words were unaccompanied by money, it does not apply. The reason being: the ultimate purpose of the Flood was to fortify the legal acquisition of existence; for previously creation held no legal claim, having been brought forth by mere speech (“By the word of the Lord the heavens were made”), and mere verbal agreement does not effect formal acquisition.

column11: Tikkunei Zohar, Introduction (17a, Patach Eliyahu): ‘Elijah opened and said: Master of the worlds, You are One, but not in number… Malkhut is the Mouth, which we call the Oral Torah (Torah she-be’al peh); Chokhmah is the Brain, which is the inner Thought; and Binah is the Heart, through which the heart understands.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Tikkunei Zohar 17a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and this is Malchus: "the mouth—we call it the Oral Torah" (Tikkunei Zohar 17a); and "the end of action is rooted in the initial thought," drawing sustenance from the primordial depth; for "Is not...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And in Pesachim [87b] they taught that Israel was exiled to Babylonia so they would eat dates and engage in Torah, referring to the Oral Torah established in Babylonia; as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that honey accustoms the tongue to Torah, which is why dates are termed "honey" in the Torah; and Malkhut, which is the mouth, is designated the Oral Torah (Tikkunei Zohar 17a).
column15: Only after creation endured the devastation of the Flood was this ownership firmly forged with greater power; for the essence of rectification is enabling creatures to receive the light, achieved through additional garments, alluded to in the rectifications of the Idra (Zohar Naso 135b): “to fashion glory for His glory”; and in Zohar (Balak 204b): “The primordial light shone so brilliantly that worlds could not bear it; what did the Holy One do? He fashioned light within His light to enclothe one within the other.”

And this is the healing of the loquacious tongue through Torah, turning his body into fire, as in Chagigah (27a): "Is not My word like fire, says Hashem" Jeremiah 23:29; through vital Torah speech the permutation of his soul-root becoming pure burning fire.
column15: So that when Hashem clarifies the exalted soul, He redeems the lesser soul alongside it through spiritual levirate redemption (yibbum; see Parashat Korach). For to this honoring father and mother was juxtaposed to Shabbat, to instruct us that if man errs in the refinement of his actions, which is termed Shabbat, his remedy is near at hand to fulfill honoring father and mother, rectifying the deficiency ingrained in him from the day of his birth from the root of father and mother.

column11: Exodus 24:7: ‘Then he took the record of the covenant and read it aloud to the people. column13: For Abraham sifted and purified all evil desires until he merited the Covenant in his flesh, which is the sign of that complete refinement, possessing no lust for evil, all desires being consecrated to Hashem. And this is woven into nature from birth and womb; thus by virtue of this covenantal sanctity he is not permitted to enter at all, merely standing at the portal without stumbling into the lust itself, for "your people are all righteous," and even uncircumcised Israelites are called circumcised.
column15: And this is why it is written (Exodus 24:11): “And they beheld (vayochezu) God,” rather than “and they saw (vayir'u)”; for seeing (re'iyah) denotes perception from a distance, recognizing the object as beyond reach, whereas beholding (chazayah) implies imagining an intimate grasp and hold.

column11: Shabbat 88a: ‘Rabbi Simai taught: When Israel accorded precedence to the declaration “We will do” over the declaration “We will hear,” 600,000 ministering angels came and tied two crowns to each and every member of the Jewish people, one corresponding to “We will do” and one corresponding to “We will hear.” And when the people sinned with the Golden Calf, 1,200,000 angels of destruction descended and removed them from the people, as it is stated in the wake of the sin of the Golden Calf: “And the children of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments from Mount Horeb onward” (Exodus 33:6). Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said: At Horeb they put on their ornaments, and at Horeb they removed them.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 88a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and thence Israel merited the two spiritual crowns corresponding to "we will do" and "we will hear" (Shemos 24:7; Shabbat 88a); namely corresponding to Torah and Avodah, which are the Crown of...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And this explains Shabbat (88a): at Sinai sixty myriads of ministering angels descended, crowning each Jew with two crowns, one for "we will do" and one for "we will hear," and when they made the Golden Calf, 120 myriads of destroying angels descended and stripped them away. Explanation: the crown signifies supreme stature and sovereignty, the two crowns denoting their dual mastery: for "we will do" as fulfillers of His word, and for "we will hear" as hearkeners to His voice, reigning as masters in both realms.
column15: As in Tikkunim and Zohar: “Come, let us deal wisely with them” (Exodus 1:10) parallels “Come, let us build us a city.” For Nimrod’s Tower, Nebuchadnezzar’s golden idol, and Pharaoh’s store-cities all share one character: seeking to compel divine bounty through spiritual manipulation, refusing to humble themselves under holiness; refusing the arduous toil of self-restraint, wishing to luxuriate in worldly lusts while remaining immune from divine retribution.

Which aligns with the verse (Parashat Yitro [Exodus 19:4]): "and I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself": the eagle flies high in the celestial atmosphere, the intermediate realm between heaven and earth, while you were borne above eagles' wings, brought directly unto Me, to the Supreme Realm.
column15: And to comprehend why throughout the creation narrative the term “Dibur” (harsh/direct speech) is absent, employing only “Amirah” (gentle utterance): because Dibur applies to an overt, explicit revelation, unlike Amirah which denotes quiet, whisper-like concealment; as taught in the Zohar (Emor 88b): “‘Speak (Emor) unto the priests’—Rabbi Yitzchak said: in a whisper.”

column13: Execution having been decreed against him by Pharaoh, he was spared through exile, as in repentance where willful sins become errors and then merits (Yoma 86b). For from that exile Hashem appeared to him at Mount Horeb, which drew Moses as a lodestone draws metal (Zohar II, 21a). And specifically through exile he reached that mountain, nothing occurring by chance, meriting that sanctuary through his wandering [after the teaching: "Who is wise? He who recognizes his place" (Avot 6:6), attaining sublime wisdom].
column15: Meaning, while enslaved in Egypt Israel was enfolded in Hashem like an unborn child, needing the Name Elohim to shield them. Afterward, however, it is written: “That the Lord (Havayah) had brought Israel out of Egypt,” upon which the Zohar states: “This Name brought them forth.”

column11: Rosh Hashanah 2a: ‘MISHNA: They are four days in the year that serve as the New Year, each for a different purpose: On the first of Nisan is the New Year for kings; it is from this date that the years of a king’s rule are counted. And the first of Nisan is also the New Year for the order of the Festivals, as it determines which is considered the first Festival of the year and which the last. On the first of Elul is the New Year for animal tithes; all the animals born prior to that date belong to the previous tithe year and are tithed as a single unit, whereas those born after that date belong to the next tithe year. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say: The New Year for animal tithes is on the first of Tishrei.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Rosh Hashanah 2a) to illuminate his exposition here (“being the New Year for kings and festivals (Rosh Hashanah 2a) in Soul (Nefesh) and Time (Shanah); the sanctity wherein Israel sanctify the seasons (Berachos 49a); and likewise for kings: "you...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Berakhot 49a: ‘Levi cited two other blessings: Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons. It means: Who sanctifies Israel, who sanctify the seasons. Who sanctifies Israel and the New Moon. column15: “He established the heavens by understanding”—meaning that in the heavens beings consciously recognize the glory of the Blessed Name who guides them. For “heavens” signify lucid clarity; hence their root is Binah (Understanding), stationed just below Chochmah, where man can consciously perceive divine glory, since human comprehension begins within the realm of Binah.

column11: Avodah Zarah 2b: ‘And Rabbi Yoḥanan says: This teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, took the Torah around to every nation and those who speak every language, such as the Edomites in Seir and the Ishmaelites in Paran, but they did not accept it, until He came to the Jewish people and they accepted it. column13: And this was Abraham's first trial—surrendering his physical life to Hashem in the furnace of Ur—representing the beginning of rational human exertion ("the former things"), through which he ascended until after the tenth trial where he cleaved to Hashem far above human reason. And this explains why the test of the nations occurred through the Sukkah, where they kicked it: for they knew that Hashem who commanded them was the very One who scorched them with the sun, which defied human reason: if You commanded it, You should accept our effort; wherefore they kicked it because it conflicted with intellect.

column11: Micah 7:15: ‘I will show him wondrous deedsAs in the days when You sallied forth from the land of Egypt.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Micah 7:15) to illuminate his exposition here (“And regarding the future redemption it is written: "According to the days of your coming out of the land of Egypt will I show him marvelous things (ar'enu nifla'ot)" (Michah 7:15); meaning when it...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: This applies universally except regarding sacrificial holy offerings (kodashim), where we maintain that night follows day; for one who has already entered the realm of holiness has day first, like one standing inside the fruit for whom the fruit precedes the peel and therefore one might initially have thought this should apply to the recitation of Shema as well, as I wrote elsewhere.
column15: And so too regarding the matter of Shabbat, where Tractate Shabbat (73a) enumerates the creative labors of preparing bread and garments wherein man must restrain himself, in truth Shabbat alludes to the ultimate future, as taught in the Gemara (Shabbat 30b): “In the future the Land of Israel will bring forth ready-baked rolls and fine woolen garments,” meaning sustenance and clothing without wearisome toil.

column11: Sanhedrin 97b: ‘§ Rav says: All the ends of days that were calculated passed, and the matter depends only upon repentance and good deeds. When the Jewish people repent, they will be redeemed. And Shmuel says: It is sufficient for the mourner to endure in his mourning to bring about the coming of the Messiah. Even without repentance, they will be worthy of redemption due to the suffering they endured during the exile. The Gemara notes: This dispute is parallel to a dispute between tanna’im: Rabbi Eliezer says: If the Jewish people repent they are redeemed, and if not they are not redeemed.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 97b) to illuminate his exposition here (“meaning when it arrives "in its time" (b'itah) without prior merit, even though the Holy One will set up a king as harsh as Haman so that they repent (Sanhedrin 97b); that repentance will be...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: Therefore there exists within them as well the root of the holiness of Israel which can never be severed, and on account of this root the name of Israel remains upon him, so that his marriage is legally binding; and even if he does not repent during his lifetime, he will ultimately repent at his death; as it is taught [in Eruvin 19a] that the sinners of Israel justify the divine judgment upon themselves in Gehinnom, declaring: "You have judged rightly, etc.".
column15: And there is one who arrives later in the world, acquiring those profound Torah concepts through the stumbling that occurred prior to his existence: as occurred with the shattered worlds before creation, Hashem building and destroying worlds until creating this one, saying: “This one pleases Me”; and surely Hashem never repents of His deeds, for He is not a man that He should repent.

column11: Shabbat 151b: ‘It was also taught in a baraita with regard to the appreciation of life: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: Perform mitzvot while you still find opportunities, and you have the financial means, and you are still under your own control. And King Solomon also said, in his wisdom: “And remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years arrive when you will say: I have no desire for them” (Ecclesiastes 12:1). Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar explains: “The evil days”; these are the days of old age. “And the years arrive when you will say: I have no desire for them”; these are the days of Messiah, in which there is neither merit nor liability.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 151b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and the wonder does not point to what will manifest in the Messianic era, which will be days without free choice; wherefore it is termed nifla'ot in the plural, denoting wonders of wonders; for...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And by this name is the spiritual force of the Eshet Zenunim in the cosmos designated, as stated in Shabbat (151b): "One who sleeps alone in a house is seized by Lilith"—meaning that he experiences a nocturnal emission, for this represents the ultimate craving of the Eshet Zenunim. And this power of lust in the world spreads into an individual during his sleep, and through the sheer intensity of that subconscious arousal he experiences an emission in his dream, as is known; and during sleep, his conscious intellect is not active to subdue his inclination through his wisdom, allowing that invasive desire to execute its effect.
column15: At which point they halted, unable to emerge. This was because up to the surface of the ground, creation does not enter the realm of human choice, and no fear exists of acting contrary to His will; but upon bursting forth into the open air of the world, undergoing a complete transformation of form, they fall under the domain of man who possesses free will and can do with them as he pleases.

column11: Pesachim 116b: ‘The tanna of the mishna further states: In each and every generation a person must view himself as though he personally left Egypt, as it is stated: “And you shall tell your son on that day, saying: It is because of this which the Lord did for me when I came forth out of Egypt” (Exodus 13:8). "Vayakam"): that the Generation of the Dispersion reincarnated in the generation of the wilderness who departed Egypt.

column11: Berakhot 34b: ‘And Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: All the prophets only prophesied with regard to the change in world order in the end of days with regard to the days of the Messiah. However, with regard to the World-to-Come, which exists on a higher level, it is stated: “No eye has seen it, God, aside from You.” And the Gemara notes that this statement disagrees with the opinion of Shmuel, as Shmuel said: The only difference between this world and the days of the Messiah is with regard to servitude to foreign kingdoms alone. While in the days of the Messiah, Israel will be independent and free from enslavement to foreign powers, the world order will remain otherwise unchanged, as it is stated: “For the poor shall not cease from the land” (Deuteronomy 15:11), which indicates that the ways of the world are set and unchanging.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 34b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and nevertheless it was revealed to the prophets, who all prophesied concerning the days of Mashiach (Berachos 34b); that although they did not perceive the light in concrete reality as it will be...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And from the side of this world, even the words of the opinion there [Berachos 34b] — that all the prophets prophesied only for baalei teshuvah, etc. — are true, for “these and those are the words of the living God.” And from the side of what is apprehended by the prophets, the rank of the baalei teshuvah is lower than the completely righteous — for this rung of teshuvah is not apprehended from the side of prophecy at all, as R’ Yochanan himself said there, “all the prophets prophesied only for the days of Mashiach, but of the World to Come, ‘no eye has seen a God besides You who acts for the one who waits for Him’ (Yeshayah 64:3).”
column15: “The eye of a fine needle”—this denotes a minute aperture of pure radiance through which the cleft (sedek)—the concealing rift dividing the universe from God's light—could be bridged; through it they would perceive that there is no autonomous innovation in creation, for the Blessed Name alone is One, and nothing exists in reality aside from Him alone.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 43:2: ‘“Abram heard that his brother had been taken captive” – that is what is written: “He seals his ears from hearing of bloodshed” (Isaiah 33:15). “He marshaled [vayarek] his disciples” – Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Neḥemya, Rabbi Yehuda says: Their faces turned pale [horiku] towards Abraham. They said: ‘Five kings could not overcome them, and [you think] we will be able to overcome them?’ Rabbi Neḥemya said: Abraham turned pale [horik] towards them. He said: ‘Shall I go and fall [in battle] in sanctification of the name of the Omnipresent?’ Abba bar Zavda said: He armed them with weapons, just as it says: “Unsheathe [harek] a spear to block my pursuers” (Psalms 35:3). Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: He showered them with jewels and gems, as it says: “Its pinions with shimmering [yerakrak] gold” (Psalms 68:14).…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 43:2) to illuminate his exposition here (“as the Sages stated (Bereishis Rabbah 43:2) on the verse "and pursued as far as Dan" (Bereishis 14:14); all the more so in the abundant measure of goodness: just as a sacred moment sanctifies...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: In this portion it is written: "And Malki-Tzedek king of Shalem brought out bread and wine," and it is taught (in Bereishit Rabbah 43): "Every wine mentioned in the Torah leaves a negative mark except this one," and the Matnot Kehunah explains: that a spiritual stumbling resulted, as with Noach and the sons of Aharon, and so all of them.
column15: Yet when he ceases and rests on Shabbat, gathering all the goodness acquired throughout the six workdays and elevating it into the Sabbath, as stated in the Zohar (Balak 192b) on the verse: “And rose up from Seir unto them”—from that which Seir rejected, Hashem illuminated Israel, bestowing upon them abundant light and love— meaning that Israel channels all raw vitality into holiness, serving Hashem with that power and acknowledging Him as the sole Giver.

column13: And it is known that Surrounding Light is the level of Keter, the hidden root of the source of thoughts, how they are born from Hashem's true will. And if he cleaves there to Hashem, His light encompasses him, and all thoughts and desires drawn thence are dedicated to Hashem alone. And this is tefillin, which is also a garment and Surrounding Light, but with binding and total attachment.
column15: And this is what Scripture declares of him: “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, Maker/Acquirer (koneh) of heaven and earth” — because Abraham surrendered back all worldly bounty into the hand of Hashem; giving all he had to Isaac, and offering Isaac himself as a burnt-offering unto Hashem, thereby returning all earthly blessings directly to the Blessed Name.

column15: In that moment this consciousness was born in man, falling into dread lest he possessed independent power to rebel, causing his trembling. Therefore it asks where Haman is alluded to—where it is hinted that Israel could fall into such darkness, fearing God had abandoned them; resolving from “Hamin ha-etz” and “haster astir” — meaning that when Hashem rebuked Adam, he experienced dread greater than Haman's era, Hashem rebuking him as though his eating had not been ordained.

column11: Isaiah 66:23: ‘And new moon after new moon,And sabbath after sabbath,All flesh shall come to worship Me—said GOD.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Isaiah 66:23) to illuminate his exposition here (“for of the Future it is said: "And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before Me, says Hashem" (Yeshayah...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And even within Jacob's boundless heritage: though not all ascend into the celestial Jerusalem perpetually; all Israel ascend on the Three Pilgrimage Festivals under biblical obligation (Shemos 23:17); and in the Future this pilgrimage will expand to every Sabbath and New Moon: "from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before Me, says Hashem" (Yeshayah 66:23); meriting during these sacred appointed times the boundless holiness of the World to Come beyond their individual measured portions!
column15: Then the ultimate preciousness will lie in the preparation of the receptive vessel—whoever expanded it more; for in this world man can enlarge and widen his capacity to receive through his divine service in the fear of Hashem, whereas in the future when active labor ceases—and “he who toiled on the eve of the Sabbath shall eat on the Sabbath”—true distinction will belong entirely to the vessel.

column11: Ketubot 75a: ‘§ Since the Gemara quoted a statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s grandson, the Gemara cites another exposition in his name. The verse states: “And of Zion it shall be said, this man and this man were born in her, and the Most High shall establish her” (Psalms 87:5). Rabbi Meyasha, son of the son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, said: Both the man who was actually born in Zion and the one who looks forward to seeing her are equally considered sons of Zion. Abaye said: And one of the inhabitants of Eretz Yisrael is superior to two of us, Babylonians. Rava said: And one of us Babylonians, when he ascends to Eretz Yisrael, is superior to two people born and raised in Eretz Yisrael. The Gemara cites a proof for Rava’s claim: As Rabbi Yirmeya, when he was here, in Babylonia, did not even know what the Sages say.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Ketubot 75a) to illuminate his exposition here (“along the lines of: "One of ours who goes there is worth two of theirs" (Kesubos 75a); and then the holiness of the month will be revealed upon the name of Israel who are destined to be renewed...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column15: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” This is what Scripture states (Psalms 92:1–2): “A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day: It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to sing praises to Your Name, Most High.”

column11: Sanhedrin 42a: ‘Rather, the full version of the blessing is the version of Rav Yehuda. He set for them a law and a time, that they should not deviate from their task. And they are joyous and glad to perform the will of their Owner; they are workers of truth whose work is truth. column13: And just as Hashem rules over man who accepts His kingdom, so Israel will govern the human form of the nations. Reflecting the likeness of an ape before a human, so the nations appear before Israel; and in any event they will not be annihilated, but the spirit of impurity will be banished from the earth—namely the impure spiritual body spanning the ten Sefirot in spirit alone, lacking a physical body, never having reached physical completion in deed.
column15: Why then did the Torah open with Bereishit? Only because “He declared the power of His works to His people, to give them the heritage of nations”— meaning that the Blessed Name desires to give Israel every mitzvah and holy deed from its primordial root, so that even beyond conscious intellect they may attain the sanctity of the Patriarchs.

column11: Shemot Rabbah 16:2: ‘“Draw, and take for yourselves lambs” – that is what is written: “With stillness and pleasantness you will be saved” (Isaiah 30:15). We learned: One may heal himself with anything except for idol worship, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed. How so? If they will say to a person: ‘Come and kill a person and you will be healed,’ he may not heed them, as it is written: “One who sheds the blood of a man, his blood will be shed by man” (Genesis 9:6). Since “one who sheds the blood of a man, his blood will be shed by man,” how could the ill person be healed by means of bloodshed? Forbidden sexual relations, how so? If they will say to a person: ‘Engage in forbidden sexual relations and you will be healed,’ he may not heed them, as it is prohibited for a person to engage in forbidden sexual relations.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shemot Rabbah 16:2) to illuminate his exposition here (“"Draw out your hands from idolatry and take you a lamb of mitzvah" (Shemos 12:21; Shemos Rabbah 16:2); and the illumination of the Vav [the Yud of Ehyeh], wherein was revealed in actual deed the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

The explanation is that reverent awe resides in the heart, as expounded in Yoma (72b) on the verse: "'and he has no heart'—woe to the enemies of Torah scholars who engage in Torah without fear of Heaven," see there; and likewise in Sanhedrin (106b) regarding Doeg and Ahitophel: "The Holy One, Blessed be He, desires the heart," see there.

column15: And likewise the southern wind/direction alludes to this, for spiritual light emanates from the southern side, and therefore he merited to ascend above to abide continually at the right hand of Hashem, for there is no left side on high.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 9:7: ‘Rabbi Naḥman bar Shmuel bar Naḥman said in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Naḥman: “Behold it was very good” – this is the good inclination; “and behold it was very good” – this is the evil inclination. Is the evil inclination, then, very good? This is a rhetorical question. Rather, were it not for the evil inclination, a man would never build a house, would never marry a wife, would never beget children, and would never engage in commerce. Likewise, Solomon says: “[And I have considered all toil and all excelling in work,] that it is each man’s envy of his counterpart” (Ecclesiastes 4:4).’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 9:7) to illuminate his exposition here (“after the manner of what is said (Bereishis Rabbah 9:7): "'and behold, it was very good' (Bereishis 1:31)—this refers to the yetzer hara"; for when one subdues it so that it has no dominion, it...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And there is a vital need for both day and night, as expounded in Bereishit Rabbah (chapter 9): "'And behold, it was very good'—this refers to sleep," see there; and as is known regarding the verse: "A righteous man falls seven times and rises," that descent is a prerequisite for a higher ascent. Just as we observe in fruit trees: in order to renew their youth like an eagle, the winter must first cause their leaves to wither and shed, after which the tree blossoms anew with the arrival of summer.

column11: Pesachim 112a: ‘The Gemara continues to cite similar advice dispensed by Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva commanded Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai to do five matters when Rabbi Akiva was imprisoned. column11: Sifrei Bamidbar 143: ‘(Bamidbar 28:8) "And the second lamb": Why is this written? Since it is written "the one lamb shall you offer in the morning," I might think that if it were not offered in the morning it could be offered in the evening. It is, therefore, written "the second shall you offer up towards evening," implying that if the morning tamid had not been offered, the evening tamid is not to be offered. When is this so? When the altar had not been inaugurated. But if it had been inaugurated, even the first may be offered in the evening. R. Shimon said: When is this so? column11: Bereshit Rabbah 1:1: ‘Rabbi Hoshaya the Great began: “I was with Him as an amon, a delight day after day…” (Proverbs 8:30) – amon means a child’s caretaker, amon means covered, amon means hidden, and some say amon means greatness. Amon means a child’s caretaker, as it says: “As a caretaker [omen] carries a nursing child” (Numbers 11:12). Amon means covered, as it says: “Those covered [ha’emunim] in scarlet…” (Lamentations 4:5). Amon means hidden, as it says: “He was omen Hadassa” (Esther 2:7). Amon means great, as it says: “Are you better than No Amon [which sits in the rivers]?” (Nahum 3:8), which we translate in Targum as: Are you better than the great city of Alexandria, which is located among the rivers? Another matter, amon means artisan [uman]. The Torah is saying: ‘I was the tool of craft of the Holy One blessed be He.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 1:1) to illuminate his exposition here (“And likewise the Torah which is the blueprint of Creation (Bereishis Rabbah 1:1); being the measure of His divine governance according to which the entire creation was formed in limited,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: Therefore all varied modes of divine governance innovated at creation are hinted at in their blueprint—the Torah—wherefore it enlightens human beings. And since the entire created cosmos exists for human moral development—that man might possess free choice, selecting good to serve the King of Glory, divine honor shining precisely when man can choose evil yet rejects it, which is the purpose of all creation; all varied divine paths were formed for his sake, making this wisdom relevant to man, for divine governance operates dynamically wherever multiple choices exist, which applies uniquely to human souls.
column15: It is stated in Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 1:10): Why was the world created with the letter Beit (numerically two)? To inform you that there are two worlds: this world and the World to Come. Another explanation: Why with a Beit? Because it is the language of blessing (berachah).

column11: Makkot 23b: ‘§ Rabbi Simlai taught: There were 613 mitzvot stated to Moses in the Torah, consisting of 365 prohibitions corresponding to the number of days in the solar year, and 248 positive mitzvot corresponding to the number of a person’s limbs. column13: At the conclusion of Makkot 23b: the 365 negative commandments correspond to the solar days of the year; and the 248 positive commandments correspond to the limbs of the human body. For the physical body cannot survive without food, as our Sages noted and as I wrote elsewhere, representing active mitzvot, passive avoidance of harm being insufficient; whereas the solar days were established prior to the creation of man and were already complete in their cosmic cycle, requiring only that man not corrupt them, wherefore negative prohibitions correspond to the solar days; see Tiferet Yisrael, chapter 4.
column15: Meaning that he must then embrace deep constriction, nullifying all active agency; for the supreme shield on the day of wrath derives from negative commandments: from positive commandments performed actively, man acquires internal light (or pnimi) in body and soul; whereas from negative commandments observed passively, he acquires no internalized vessel, but surrounding light (or makif) shielding him from evil.

column11: Makkot 24a: ‘§ Rabbi Simlai taught: There were 613 mitzvot stated to Moses in the Torah, consisting of 365 prohibitions corresponding to the number of days in the solar year, and 248 positive mitzvot corresponding to the number of a person’s limbs. In addition, there are two mitzvot: “I am the Lord your God” and: “You shall have no other gods” (Exodus 20:2, 3), the first two of the Ten Commandments, that we heard from the mouth of the Almighty, for a total of 613.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Makkot 24a) to illuminate his exposition here (“for behold, all of them attained the level of prophecy at Mount Sinai, hearing Anochi and Lo yihyeh lecha directly from the mouth of the Almighty (Makkos 24a); and so will they all attain this in...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: These parallel the two rungs in human divine service: as stated in Makkot (24a): "Two commandments we heard directly from the mouth of the Almighty: Anochi and Lo Yihyeh"; being two foundations for the two modes of serving Hashem: Anochi stems from revelation and lucid awareness that "I am Hashem your God," while Lo Yihyeh stems from concealment: commanding that at the very least you shall have no other gods, remaining fenced and contracted within halachic boundaries defining that this is forbidden, and this, and this.
column15: Therefore, when the commandment “Anochi” was unveiled, there was no conceptual space to state “You shall have no other” and the rest of the commandments; only after that light was gently concealed did human perception properly begin.

column11: Pesachim 56a: ‘As Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said that it is written: “And Jacob called his sons and said, Gather around and I will tell you what will occur to you in the end of days” (Genesis 49:1). Jacob wanted to reveal to his sons when the complete redemption would arrive at the end of days (see Daniel 12:13), but the Divine Presence abandoned him, rendering him unable to prophesy. He said: Perhaps the Divine Presence has abandoned me because, Heaven forfend, one of my descendants is unfit, as was the case with my grandfather Abraham, from whom Ishmael emerged, and like my father Isaac, from whom Esau emerged. His sons said to him: Hear Israel, our father, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One. They said: Just as there is only one God in your heart, so too, there is only one in our hearts.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 56a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and even regarding Yaakov Avinu whose bed was unblemished (Pesachim 56a), it was not yet verified that this held true across all his future seed: that even those submerged in the deepest immersion...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: Now, whoever does not reflect deeply on the matter might assume that this mitzvah does not need to be mentioned, since all Israel are believers, children of believers, yet even though this is true regarding the essence of faith residing in the heart, nevertheless, regarding its practical translation into physical deed, we observe the contrary, and as is also well known from what is cited in Chovot HaLevavot [at the beginning of the Gate of Trust] from the reply of the magus to that ascetic: "Your action contradicts your words,"

And for this reason they instituted at the opening: "O Lord, open my lips, etc." (Psalms 51:17), for the Name Adonai alludes to His Shechinah dwelling within the hearts of the children of Israel; and we plead that the Shechinah open the mouth, so that the mouth does not speak mechanically on its own, but solely what the heart opens, and the Holy One is the heart of Israel—"God is the rock of my heart" (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5)—which is the attribute of this Name as is known.
column15: And so it is within the human soul: in truth, it might have seemed fitting for man to be created with complete spiritual maturity for God's service; yet the Blessed Name purposefully created man lacking understanding, so that through holy toil he should resolve that deficiency; for in every soul an innate imperfection resides, as it is written (Psalms 51:7): “And in sin did my mother conceive me.”

column15: Yet because His benevolent Will yearned to bestow good upon His creatures, He established in this world that every entity be bounded by measure and boundary (and these matters are profound; examine the introduction to the holy book Beit Yaakov [Sha'ar HaEmunah], page 101, and you will understand).

This is because the pleasure a person derives from food, if channeled into the divine soul and the transcendent divine spark within him— meaning when he recognizes that the Blessed Name created this food, sustains it, grants it existence, infuses it with flavor and pleasure, and grants man the appetite to relish it and draw physical strength and vitality from it.

column11: Yoma 71a: ‘The verse states: “To you men [ishim] do I call, and my voice is to the sons of men” (Proverbs 8:4). Rabbi Berekhya said: The word ishim, although it means men, is similar to the term isha, woman. It may therefore be taken to refer to these Torah scholars, who are similar to women in that they are physically weak and are not engaged in many activities that other men are, but nevertheless, they act mightily like men when engaged in Torah study. And Rabbi Berekhya said further about that same verse: Nowadays one who wishes to pour libations of wine over the altar should fill the throats of Torah scholars with wine, as it is stated: “To you men [ishim] do I call.” The use of the phrase ishim, which is similar to isheh, used for the altar’s fire, suggests that scholars may be compared to the fire of the altar.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 71a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and so is it taught (Yoma 71a): "Whoever fills the throat of Torah scholars with wine is as if he poured wine libations upon the altar"; for their bodies are the Sanctuary of Hashem and the Altar...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column15: Meaning the brilliant clarity of heaven is mere constriction compared to His light; nevertheless, since Hashem fills all worlds, He oversees every minute detail with individual providence, certainly feeling every deed of this world.

column11: Chullin 7a: ‘He said to the river: Ginai, part your water for me and I will pass through you. column13: And Hashem, blessed be He, created man with an inescapable biological imperative to eat, leaving him only the choice of what to eat and how much to eat, but eating vegetative sustenance is an absolute physical necessity, and this natural necessity is itself termed a mitzvah, as the river Ginnai declared in the first chapter of Chullin (7a): "I am going to perform the will of my Creator," for that which Hashem established in nature constitutes His will and is therefore a mitzvah.
column15: Such that through the power of that very garment which Hashem willed to sustain, he gained the ability to expand into his lusts contrary to the true ultimate intent of the divine Will. column11: Taanit 22b: ‘Rabbi Yosei says: An individual is not permitted to afflict himself by fasting, lest he become too weak to work and be beholden to other beings, and those beings will not have mercy on him. column15: For the inward stirring within the heart is not visibly discernible, making it seem as though all human beings stand on equal footing; and the reason one individual toils and accomplishes more than his fellow stems from his bringing that inner call to conscious realization, whereby it is rightly attributed to man’s effort.

column11: Eruvin 41a: ‘And Rabbi Yosei says: He must fast and complete the fast. column15: Rabbi Chiyya said: Because on them constructive labor is permitted, hence they are not called holy; and regarding this the Sages established the Havdalah blessing dividing between holy and secular. And through man guarding the Sabbath day, never trespassing its borders nor performing mundane labor, he is subsequently enabled during the following six workdays to acquire the blessings of this world with abundant holiness.

column11: Pesachim 59b: ‘Rav Ashi said to Rav Kahana, and some say it Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan, said to Rav Pappa: But, isn’t it the case that as long as the sacrificial parts of the sin-offering have not been burned on the altar, the priests may not eat the meat? As it was taught in a baraita with regard to peace-offerings: I might have thought that the priests would be permitted to eat the breast and thigh, which are designated for them from the peace-offering, prior to burning the sacrificial parts of the offering on the altar. Therefore, the verse states: “And the priest shall burn the fat upon the altar, and the breast shall be for Aaron and his sons” (Leviticus 7:31). From here it is derived that the priest is first obligated to burn the fat, and only then: “The breast shall be for Aaron and his sons.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 59b) to illuminate his exposition here (“akin to the priests eating sacrificial meat, through which the owners achieve atonement just as through sprinkling the blood and burning the fats upon the altar (Pesachim 59b); for the Kohanim...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column15: So with sacrifices: peace-offerings (shelamim) are eaten by owners and priests, yielding internal light; burnt-offerings (olah) ascend entirely to Heaven, yielding surrounding light; yet the olah holds greater sanctity, surrounding light being higher than internal light.

column11: Zohar, Bereshit 18:204-19:217: ‘The explanation is this. God created the world by means of the Torah, that is to say, in so far as it is called Reshith. By this Reshith He created the heavens and the earth, and He supports them by it, because the word Bereshith contains the word brith (covenant); this covenant is referred to in the verse: “Were it not for my covenant with the day and night, I had not appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth” (Jer. 33, 25). This heaven is that of which it is said “the heavens are the heavens of the Lord” (Ps. 115, 16), and this earth is the “land of the living” comprising seven lands of which David said: “I will walk before the Lord in the lands of the living” (Ibid. 116, 9).’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 9, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Bereshit 18:204-19:217) to illuminate his exposition here (“And it is known that arrogance is the root of all manners of evil, which sprouted from the primordial kings who died because each of them declared: "I shall reign," as is known (Zohar I, 24b);...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And were one to imagine, Heaven forbid, the withdrawal of His influx for a single instant, all worlds and creatures would cease to exist as though they never were, the root of all actions being Hashem's essence. And this conviction is the cornerstone of Jewish faith: that nothing occurs by blind accident. Not like those who argue that once Hashem created the world He detached Himself from it and it can subsist without His active providence; nor like those who admit His providence but view it as sporadic, the cosmos persisting even when He withdraws supervision.
column15: Naming them meaning binding them to their root to recognize their purpose; as in Zohar and Bahir: “and whatsoever the man called every living creature, that was the name thereof”—that was its essence. Adam bound them to their root, revealing why they were created; vegetation not receiving names because it was on a lower plane, requiring elevation through human consumption into the human form.

column11: Gittin 13a: ‘The Gemara raises a difficulty: On the contrary, by emancipating him the master renders it permitted for him to engage in sexual intercourse with a free woman. column13: And this is what Scripture states: 'after all the desire of your soul you may eat meat,' for meat is needed to gladden the heart and straighten it; and it is written: 'When Hashem your God shall enlarge your border, etc.,' that one should not eat meat except out of broad financial capability and wealth, as Rashi explains, and similar to what is written in the Gemara (Chullin 84a); meaning that he to whom Hashem granted wealth and possessions certainly requires meat and wine for Torah and divine service.

column15: Different was the Generation of the Dispersion who grasped merely the outward habit, namely the final external garment of this attribute, in that their primary motivation in making one band was that through this Hashem would channel unto them all bounties, and once Hashem's bounty was given they would expand into it according to their lust and selfish heart's desire.
